name: ASKARI
excerpt: We get asked this a lot: why defense, why counter-robot, why now, and why us. The answer starts long before Askari.
body: We get asked this a lot: why defense, why counter-robot, why now, and why us.

The answer starts long before Askari. Robbie was building drones in a garage just south of Atlanta as a kid, racing quads at 80 miles an hour before he could drive, founding a high school drone team, winning nationals, then going to Georgia Tech and Skydio to learn what autonomous systems could do when you stopped treating them like toys. Marc came up through that same world, captained the team after Robbie left, won nationals again, and studied computer science at Georgia Tech because he understood early that the future of flight would belong to software as much as hardware. Ben came through Raytheon and saw the inside of the legacy defense machine firsthand: the budgets, the timelines, the inertia, and the logic of building expensive answers for a world that had already changed. Ben and Robbie had already built together before, winning robotics competitions at Georgia Tech, moving fast, breaking things, and learning by doing. None of us came to this as consultants, spectators, or people interested in writing memos about what someone else should build. We came to it as engineers who grew up making things fly, roll, crawl and who now feel a responsibility to make sure the wrong things do not.

That responsibility became impossible to ignore because the economics of modern conflict have changed. A drone now costs less than a laptop. It can carry a payload, navigate autonomously, and operate in a swarm. You do not need a nation state budget to field one. You do not need a PhD to use one. In many cases, you need a credit card, basic parts, and an afternoon. The traditional answer from the defense establishment is often a missile that costs millions of dollars. That is not a real answer. It is an outdated cost structure trying to solve a new problem with old math. In the summer of 2025, we stood in a field in North Dakota demonstrating a counter drone system for the Department of Homeland Security. We were the youngest team there by decades, and we were also the cheapest solution in the field. That was not a coincidence. It was proof of the principle that defines everything we do: the threat is cheap, so the answer has to be cheaper.

That is why now matters. Every year you wait, hostile autonomous systems get better and less expensive. Sensors shrink. Compute accelerates. Flight controllers improve. The line between hobbyist capability and military capability keeps collapsing. This is not a future problem. It is already here. Drones have flown over military bases, stadiums, and critical infrastructure that still lacks an effective way to say no. Ukraine showed the world that cheap autonomous systems can reshape the battlefield. The next proof will not stay overseas forever. The window between when this threat becomes obvious and when it becomes unmanageable is small, and we intend to act inside it.

That is why we built Askari. Askari means guard, soldier, protector. We chose the name Askari because this company is not about next-generation technology. It is about what technology protects. We believe democracy, infrastructure, and civilian life should not be left exposed to the logic of cheap robotic violence. Our mission is to make every hostile robot a bad investment. It is the single most important constraint that governs every product decision we make. If something does not make the economics worse for the attacker and better for the defender, it does not ship. Our culture resembles the ethos of our defense customers: we believe the best ideas come from people who build fast, test in the real world, and do not wait for permission. We set up shop in one of Atlanta's oldest industrial buildings because this work lives in the physical world, and history reminds us of the lessons previous generations learned the hard way.

What matters most is that low-cost robotic intelligence is no longer hypothetical. Machines can already sense, decide, and act at scale. The question is whether the people building defensive systems move fast enough to keep that capability from being used to coerce, destabilize, and destroy. We do not see this as a market trend or a narrow business opportunity. We see it as a civilizational obligation. What gets built in this window, by teams willing to face the problem honestly, will shape whether robotic violence becomes the noise of this century or whether it is constrained early and made economically irrational. We choose the second.
We are three engineers from Georgia, and in many ways we have been building toward this our entire lives.
We just did not know it yet.

name: HYPEPOTAMUS
topic: The Atlanta Startup Racing to Build Defenses Against the Next Terror Threat: Robotic Warfare
excerpt: Askari Defense wants to be the Southeast's go-to defense company, bringing unlimited kinetic defense to life. The Georgia Tech-born startup is emerging from stealth with autonomous counter-drone systems designed to make every hostile robot a bad investment.

name: TECH SQUARE ATL
topic: Now Out of Stealth, Askari Is Building Smarter, Decentralized Defense Systems
excerpt: A new defense technology startup is emerging from stealth with a distinct perspective on a rapidly evolving problem. Askari Defense is developing systems designed to counter autonomous machines, beginning with drones but extending into a broader category of robotic threats.

name: DHS S&T
topic: Taking Nefarious Drones Out of the Fight
excerpt: Askari Defense was one of ten companies selected to demonstrate kinetic counter-UAS capabilities at Camp Grafton, North Dakota, alongside defense primes like Lockheed Martin, Epirus, and BlueHalo. The DHS Science & Technology Directorate organized the multi-week evaluation to test drone-on-drone systems, directed energy weapons, and GNSS jamming for domestic homeland security use. Being in that lineup puts Askari's autonomous interceptor technology directly in the federal evaluation pipeline shaping the future of C-UAS procurement.

name: CREATE-X
excerpt: Askari is featured among the startups showcased through Georgia Tech's CREATE-X Startup Launch program, the accelerator that has produced over $2B in startup valuations across its history. Demo Day is where Georgia Tech's most ambitious student-founded ventures go live in front of investors, mentors, and industry leaders. Askari's presence in this cohort marks our origin story , the moment autonomous counter-drone defense went from thesis to company.
